---
title: "Modulo: Group Numbers by Remainder"
description: "An interview maths technique with symbols, numbers and an independent proof."
---

## When this technique appears

When detecting multiples, cycles, divisibility or equal-prefix residues.

## The question

**Why do equal remainders prove that their difference is divisible by k?**

## Formula worth memorising

$$
a\equiv b\pmod k\ \Longrightarrow\ k\mid(a-b)
$$

**Every symbol explained:** a and b are integers; k is a positive modulus; ≡ means equal remainders on division by k; k∣(a−b) means a−b is an integer multiple of k.

**Substitute actual numbers:** For a=17,b=5,k=4, both remainders are 1. Their difference is 12=4×3, so divisible by 4. If two prefix sums have the same remainder modulo 4, the subarray between them sums to a multiple of 4.

## Prove the mathematical step

Write a=qk+r and b=pk+r with the same remainder r. Subtract: a−b=(q−p)k, so k divides the difference. This turns divisibility into equal-prefix bucket lookups.

## Common mistake or limitation

For negative values, `%` can have language-specific sign conventions. Normalise a residue to 0..k−1 when using dictionary keys across implementations.

## The 20-second memory card

**Memorise: Difference divisible by k ⇔ equal residues mod k. Use prefix remainders to find divisible subarrays.**

Practise by speaking the argument, not reciting the formula alone.

**Interview problems:** Subarray Sums Divisible by K; Continuous Subarray Sum.

**Research reference:** [See the underlying method](https://cp-algorithms.com/algebra/module-inverse.html). The worked examples and explanation are original.
